what_it_does: Text-to-image diffusion models — the kind that turn a written description into a picture — come in fast-but-lower-quality variants and slow-but-high-quality variants. A serving system running only the heavy model wastes compute on simple requests; running only the light model disappoints users with complex prompts. DiffServe routes each incoming image request through a fast lightweight model first, then uses a learned quality judge to decide whether that result is good enough or needs to be redone by the heavier model, and dynamically adjusts how many GPUs are assigned to each model as traffic rises and falls.
method_in_detail:
The idea. For 20-40% of text prompts, a fast one-step diffusion model (like SD-Turbo, which takes 0.1 seconds) produces an image as good as a 50-step model (like SDv1.5, which takes 1.78 seconds). If a system could reliably identify those easy prompts and short-circuit them, it could serve far more requests per second without hurting average quality.

How the judge works. DiffServe trains a small image classifier (EfficientNet-V2, which adds only about 10 ms of overhead) to distinguish real photographs from AI-generated images. It is trained on real images labeled 'real' and on outputs from both the lightweight and heavyweight models labeled 'fake.' At serving time, after the lightweight model generates an image, the classifier outputs a confidence score: how likely does this image look like a real photograph? A high score means it is good enough to return to the user. Counterintuitively, using heavyweight model outputs as 'real' training examples hurts the classifier — only ground-truth photos work well as the 'real' class.

How resources are allocated. A central controller periodically solves a Mixed Integer Linear Program (MILP — an optimization over a mix of whole-number and continuous variables). The objective is to maximize the quality threshold while satisfying: (a) latency constraints (execution time plus estimated queue wait time from Little's Law, which says wait time equals queue length divided by arrival rate) and (b) throughput constraints (number of GPUs times per-GPU throughput must exceed estimated demand). Demand is estimated with an exponentially weighted moving average. The MILP takes about 10 ms to solve and runs off the critical path.

The key design choice. Using real photographs as the training target for the judge — not generated images — produces a classifier that correlates with human-perceived quality rather than just comparing one AI style to another.

The result. DiffServe achieves up to 24% better image quality (lower FID score) and 19-70% fewer latency deadline violations compared to state-of-the-art serving systems.
